mainEntity.name: Are stores required to show unit prices?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the state. NIST Handbook 130 publishes a model unit pricing regulation, and some states or retailers follow it or similar rules, but there is no single US federal requirement. Where shown, the shelf label gives the price per a set unit such as an ounce or 100 sheets.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between ounces and fluid ounces?

acceptedAnswer.text: An ounce measures weight (about 28.35 g) and a fluid ounce measures volume (about 29.57 mL). They are not interchangeable: 16 fl oz of honey weighs roughly 22 to 24 oz. That is why this tool compares weight, volume and count separately.

mainEntity.name: How do I compare paper towels or toilet paper fairly?

acceptedAnswer.text: Roll names such as "mega" or "double" are not standard. Compare the total sheet count, or total area, printed on the pack: price ÷ (rolls × sheets per roll). Use the Count option and enter the total sheets.

mainEntity.name: Is the bigger pack always cheaper per unit?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not always. Bulk packs are usually cheaper per unit, but promotions, store brands and multi-buy deals can make a smaller pack the better value. That is what the comparison is for.

mainEntity.name: How is the shrinkflation percentage worked out?

acceptedAnswer.text: If the price stays the same and the pack shrinks, the price per unit rises by old size ÷ new size − 1. A 16 oz pack that becomes 14.5 oz raises the price per ounce by 10.34%.
